result.question: What real-time and near-real-time data sources exist for building a live Formula 1 telemetry dashboard in 2026? Cover: (1) the official F1 Live Timing SignalR feed and how it's accessed, (2) the OpenF1 API (real-time and historical endpoints, latency, rate limits, cost), (3) the FastF1 Python library and its live timing client, (4) what specific telemetry and timing data is actually available live during a race — car telemetry (speed, throttle, brake, gear, RPM, DRS), GPS/position data, tire compounds and age, sector times, gaps/intervals, lap times, pit stops, race control messages, weather, driver standings — and which of these are truly live vs delayed vs post-session only, (5) known broadcast delay between the live data feed and TV broadcasts, and techniques for buffering/delaying a data stream for manual sync with a TV broadcast, (6) legal/terms-of-service considerations for consuming these feeds for personal use. Prioritize technical specifics: exact endpoints, data schemas, update frequencies, and Python/JavaScript libraries that consume them.
result.summary: Three main data pathways exist for a live F1 telemetry dashboard in 2026. (1) The official F1 Live Timing feed, an undocumented SignalR service — legacy classic ASP.NET endpoint https://livetiming.formula1.com/signalr (hub "Streaming", method "Subscribe") and the newer ASP.NET Core endpoint wss://livetiming.formula1.com/signalrcore (requiring F1-account auth as of the 2025 Dutch GP) — which exposes ~20 named topics including CarData.z (car telemetry), Position.z (GPS), TimingData/TimingStats/TimingAppData, WeatherData, RaceControlMessages, TrackStatus, and LapCount, with .z channels DEFLATE-compressed. (2) The FastF1 Python library, whose SignalRClient consumes this feed but only records raw text for post-session processing via Session.load() — it cannot analyze in real time; its telemetry schema gives Speed (km/h), RPM, nGear, Throttle (0-100%), Brake (bool), DRS (int), and X/Y/Z position in 1/10 m plus OnTrack/OffTrack status. (3) The OpenF1 API (openf1.org), a free/open-source REST API where historical data (2023+) is free with no auth, while real-time data (~3s latency, faster than TV) requires a paid "Sponsor" tier at EUR 9.90/month unlocking REST/MQTT/WebSocket; car_data streams speed/throttle/brake/RPM/gear/DRS at ~3.7 Hz, with intervals/positions updating ~every 4 s and stints giving tyre compound/age. Broadcast is delayed 30-60 s behind the data feed, so third-party tools (undercut-f1, matteocelani/f1-telemetry) add a configurable delay buffer (up to ~3 minutes) to manually sync data to the TV.

findings.claim: The official F1 Live Timing feed uses the SignalR protocol with two known endpoints: the legacy classic-ASP.NET https://livetiming.formula1.com/signalr (hub 'Streaming', method 'Subscribe') and the newer ASP.NET Core wss://livetiming.formula1.com/signalrcore, to which FastF1 migrated (with F1-account auth) around the 2025 Dutch GP.
findings.evidence: FastF1 client.py contains verbatim _connection_url = 'wss://livetiming.formula1.com/signalrcore' and _negotiate_url = '.../signalrcore/negotiate'; PR #760 and Issue #753 document the migration from classic to core SignalR. Troftu/F1-SignalR and the dweik.xyz writeup independently document the legacy https://livetiming.formula1.com/signalr endpoint with hub 'Streaming' and Subscribe method. Multiple independent implementations (FastF1, OpenF1.Data, F1client) corroborate. The endpoint is undocumented/unofficial but technically consistent.

findings.claim: The live feed exposes ~20 named subscribable topics including CarData.z (car telemetry), Position.z (GPS/position), TimingData, TimingStats, TimingAppData (tyre/stint data), WeatherData, RaceControlMessages, TrackStatus, DriverList, SessionInfo, and LapCount; the compressed .z channels are decoded with raw DEFLATE.
findings.evidence: FastF1's self.topics list contains exactly 20 topics (Heartbeat, AudioStreams, DriverList, ExtrapolatedClock, RaceControlMessages, SessionInfo, SessionStatus, TeamRadio, TimingAppData, TimingStats, TrackStatus, WeatherData, Position.z, CarData.z, ContentStreams, SessionData, TimingData, TopThree, RcmSeries, LapCount). Troftu/F1-SignalR independently subscribes to the same core set. matteocelani/f1-telemetry README states 'Compressed channels (CarData.z, Position.z) are decoded with raw DEFLATE.'

findings.claim: FastF1's SignalRClient can only record raw live-timing text to a file during a session; it cannot do real-time processing or analysis. The recorded data must be processed after the session via fastf1.core.Session.load(livedata=...).
findings.evidence: Primary docs and source docstring state verbatim: 'The data will be saved in a raw text format without any postprocessing. It is not possible to use this data during a session' and 'It is not possible to do real-time processing of the data.' Workflow is record-then-load-later. This is a significant limitation for a live dashboard built purely on FastF1.

findings.claim: FastF1's telemetry schema exposes core car channels — Speed (float, km/h), RPM (float), nGear (int gear), Throttle (float 0-100%), Brake (bool), DRS (int indicator) — plus GPS position as X/Y/Z floats in 1/10-meter units with an OnTrack/OffTrack Status flag, sufficient for a live car-position map.
findings.evidence: Official FastF1 docs (v3.8.x) confirm each field/type/unit verbatim. Caveat: Throttle can return a sentinel value (e.g. 104) when unavailable/stationary, and historical dtype inconsistencies were flagged in issue #601, but current docs affirm the stated types.

findings.claim: OpenF1 is a free, open-source REST API for F1 data; historical data (2023 onward) is free with no authentication, while real-time/live data during sessions requires a paid 'Sponsor' subscription at EUR 9.90/month (via Stripe) that adds REST, MQTT, and WebSocket push access.
findings.evidence: Primary site/docs state 'Historical data (from 2023 onwards) is free and accessible without authentication' and 'Real-time data requires [a paid subscription]' at EUR 9.90/month adding live access via REST/MQTT/WebSocket. Data is classified live from 30 min before to 30 min after a session, then becomes free historical. Free tier rate limit ~3 req/s (30 req/min); Sponsor ~6 req/s (60 req/min), up to 10 concurrent MQTT/WebSocket connections.

findings.claim: OpenF1 real-time data updates ~3 seconds after live events (the project claims this is faster than most TV broadcasts). Car telemetry (/v1/car_data) — speed km/h, throttle %, brake 0-100, RPM, gear 1-8, DRS — samples at ~3.7 Hz; GPS via /v1/location (3D Cartesian x/y/z at ~3.7 Hz) and /v1/position; tyre compound/age via /v1/stints; gaps/intervals via /v1/intervals updated ~every 4 s during races. About 18 endpoints total also cover laps/sector times, pit stops, team radio, weather, race control, and standings.
findings.evidence: Primary docs confirm each endpoint path, field, sample rate, and cadence verbatim: car_data '~3.7 Hz'; intervals 'Available during races only, with updates approximately every 4 seconds'; stints expose 'compound' and 'tyre_age_at_start'; FAQ states real-time updates '~3 seconds after live events — faster than most TV broadcasts' (self-reported, not independently benchmarked). Note: car_data 'may not be available in live sessions, being published shortly thereafter.'

findings.claim: Data truly available live during a race spans positions, gaps/intervals, sector times and micro-sector segments, last/best lap times, tyre compound and age, pit stops, driver status, speed-trap rankings, weather (air/track temp, wind, humidity, rainfall), DRS, and race control messages (flags, safety car, investigations, penalties, lap deletions, steward decisions), plus a live track-map position.
findings.evidence: undercut-f1 and matteocelani/f1-telemetry READMEs enumerate these live-displayed categories, each mapping to a documented SignalR topic (positions=Position.z/TimingData, sector/segments=TimingData, tyres=TimingAppData, speed traps=TimingStats BestSpeeds I1/I2/FL/ST, pit=PitLaneTimeCollection, weather=WeatherData, race control=RaceControlMessages) and corroborated by OpenF1 endpoint fields. Caveat: undercut-f1's DRS indicator and live track map require an F1 TV subscription during live sessions.

findings.claim: F1 TV/live broadcasts lag the live data feed by an indeterminate 30-60 seconds, so consuming tools implement a configurable delay buffer to manually sync data to the TV — undercut-f1 lets you add ~50 s of delay (adjustable in 1/5/30 s steps), and matteocelani/f1-telemetry buffers up to ~3 minutes; the latter also batches all channels into 50 ms windows before WebSocket broadcast on ws://localhost:8080.
findings.evidence: undercut-f1 README: 'F1 live broadcasts are usually delayed by some indeterminable amount (usually 30-60 seconds), so the TUI allows you to delay the data being displayed' with M/N delay actions. matteocelani/f1-telemetry: dashboard 'can be held back by up to three minutes so it stays in sync with your TV broadcast'; backend batches channels in 50 ms windows and rebroadcasts over ws://localhost:8080. Technique: hold the incoming stream in a time-buffered queue and release each message after a user-set offset.

findings.claim: Established reference implementations exist to build on: FastF1 (Python, reverse-engineered the SignalR stream), undercut-f1 (.NET/C# TUI built on FastF1's work), and matteocelani/f1-telemetry (Next.js/Node.js monorepo that decodes the SignalR feed and rebroadcasts it as WebSockets).
findings.evidence: undercut-f1 README credits FastF1 for 'understanding the SignalR stream coming from the F1 Live Timing service' and is 'heavily inspired by the FastF1 project.' matteocelani/f1-telemetry tagline: 'A Next.js/Node.js monorepo decoding the official SignalR feed into real-time WebSockets.' These give JavaScript and .NET consumption paths in addition to FastF1's Python client, and Troftu/F1-SignalR is an additional independent reference.

result.caveats: The legal/terms-of-service question (item 6 of the research brief) is NOT covered by any surviving verified claim — no source addressed whether consuming the official F1 SignalR feed for personal use complies with F1's terms. Treat this as unresolved. The official F1 Live Timing SignalR feed is entirely undocumented/unofficial and reverse-engineered; F1 changed its authentication/endpoint (classic to ASP.NET Core, now requiring an F1 account login) around the 2025 Dutch GP, so access methods are volatile and could break without notice — the two endpoints and auth requirements are the most time-sensitive facts here. OpenF1's ~3-second latency and 'faster than TV' claim are self-reported by the project, not independently benchmarked. Several implementation-detail claims (50 ms batching, up-to-3-minute buffer, ws://localhost:8080) rest on single secondary GitHub-README sources describing their own tools; they are accurate for those projects but are project-specific design choices, not properties of the F1 feed itself. Pricing (EUR 9.90/mo) and rate limits for OpenF1 are current as of 2026 but subject to change.
openQuestions: What are the exact legal/terms-of-service constraints for consuming the undocumented F1 Live Timing SignalR feed for personal (non-commercial) use — does F1 prohibit it, and does OpenF1's paid tier redistribute data under a license?

What exactly does the new signalrcore endpoint's F1-account authentication flow require (token acquisition, whether a paid F1 TV subscription is needed), and is the legacy /signalr endpoint still functional in 2026 or fully deprecated?

What is the precise raw message schema/format of each SignalR topic (e.g., the JSON structure of TimingData deltas and the exact DEFLATE-decoded layout of CarData.z/Position.z payloads) needed to parse the stream without FastF1?
How much of the 30-60 s broadcast delay is fixed vs. variable per broadcaster/region, and is there a reliable automated way to auto-sync the data buffer to the TV rather than manual adjustment?
